**Question 1 — division of work and ordering.**

| Files | Findings |
|---|---|
| `pipeline/run_batch.py` | F-04, F-07, F-13, F-14 (+ F-12's test targets it) |
| `pipeline/rubric.py` | F-01 (+ F-11's test targets it) |
| `pipeline/registry.py` | F-02, F-05, F-09 |
| `pipeline/score.py` | F-06, F-08 |
| `prompts/refusal.txt`, `prompts/grading_system.txt` | F-03, F-10 |
| `tests/` | F-11, F-12 |

I would run a short triage phase first, then fan out four parallel streams, then a small second wave.

**Phase 0 — triage before anyone is assigned anything (lead + reviewer, under an hour).** Merge F-04 and F-13 into one ticket (they are the same bug: `pages()` at `pipeline/run_batch.py:14-18` computes `n_pages = total // PAGE_SIZE` and yields only full pages, so the trailing partial page is silently dropped — F-04 describes the mechanism, F-13 the observed symptom). Close F-08 as stale (see question 3). Send four questions out: target values for F-06, scope for F-07, the canonical refusal-rubric name for F-03, and the real `aurora-1` endpoint for F-02. Finally, deal with the fact I verified in step 9: `tests/test_score.py::test_full_credit` fails on an untouched checkout (`assert 0.0 == 1.0`, because `Rubric.match_ratio` does a naive substring check and the criterion string "mentions the export button" never appears in the answer). That failure is in no finding, but it must be fixed — or at least filed and explicitly acknowledged — before parallel work starts, because a red baseline destroys everyone's ability to tell their regressions from pre-existing breakage.

**Wave 1 — four parallel streams, partitioned strictly by file so no two engineers ever edit the same file:**

- **Engineer A — `pipeline/run_batch.py` (the hot spot):** F-04/F-13 (fix `pages()` to yield the final partial page), then F-12 (the pagination boundary test — exact multiple of `PAGE_SIZE`, plus one extra row — placed in a new `tests/test_run_batch.py`), then F-14 (change `run_batch.py:27` to log only `row.get("id")`, not the full payload). Four of the fourteen findings live in this 29-line file; giving them all to one owner converts guaranteed merge conflicts into a simple sequence. F-12 and F-04/13 belong to the same person for a second reason: the test is the acceptance criterion for the fix (write it failing, fix, watch it pass).
- **Engineer B — `pipeline/rubric.py`:** F-01 (join multi-line criteria in `Rubric.parse`, `rubric.py:9-11`, which currently keeps only lines starting with `-` and drops continuation lines), then F-11 (edge-case parse tests — empty lines, nested dashes — in a new `tests/test_rubric.py`). Same fix-plus-its-test pairing.
- **Engineer C — `pipeline/registry.py`:** F-09 immediately (`DEFAULT_DATASET` at `registry.py:11` points at `fixtures/eval_set_2025.jsonl`, which does not exist; `fixtures/eval_set.jsonl` does), then F-02 and F-05 as soon as triage supplies the endpoint URL and confirms the v3 rubric identifier. These are three one-line edits in an 11-line file that nothing else imports (verified by grep), so they are trivially safe — but only if one person owns the file.
- **Engineer D — prompts:** F-10 immediately (add the cite-your-criterion instruction to `prompts/grading_system.txt`), F-03 when the rubric name arrives (`prompts/refusal.txt`). Text-only, zero code coupling. D can also add the F-08 regression test pinning the null/empty-scores-zero behavior of `score.py:6-9`.

**Wave 2 — decision-gated items, after answers land:** F-06 (replace `PARTIAL_CREDIT_THRESHOLDS` at `score.py:3` with the agreed values, plus test updates) goes to whoever frees up first — nobody else touches `score.py` in wave 1 once F-08 is closed. F-07 goes to Engineer A only, after F-04/13 has merged, because whatever "apply MAX_CONCURRENCY" turns into will restructure the same loop the pagination fix just changed.

The ordering logic in one line: triage first because the backlog as written contains a duplicate, a stale item, and two undecided items — fanning out before fixing that guarantees wasted work; within streams, fixes and their covering tests are sequenced under one owner; across streams order doesn't matter, which is exactly what the file-based partition buys.

**Question 2 — risks of parallelizing, and what in this backlog creates them.**

1. **Single-file contention in `pipeline/run_batch.py`.** Four findings (F-04, F-07, F-13, F-14) plus F-12's test all target one 29-line file. A naive one-finding-per-engineer split puts three or four people in it simultaneously — textual merge conflicts at minimum.
2. **Duplicate assignment of the same bug.** F-04 and F-13 are one defect described twice (I verified both point at the `pages()` remainder drop). Handed to two engineers, you get two competing rewrites of the same function, and the second merge either conflicts or silently double-applies.
3. **Semantic (not just textual) conflict between F-07 and F-04/F-13.** "Applying" `MAX_CONCURRENCY` means restructuring the sequential loop in `run()` (`run_batch.py:21-29`). Done concurrently with the pagination fix by a different person, a concurrency refactor can reintroduce the dropped-tail bug or change result ordering (`results` currently preserves input order) even if git merges cleanly.
4. **The red baseline poisons everyone's signal.** `tests/test_score.py::test_full_credit` fails on a clean checkout (verified: `assert 0.0 == 1.0`). Every engineer running tests before their first change sees a failure they didn't cause; the F-06 owner, editing `score.py`, is especially likely to burn time thinking they broke it — or worse, a real regression hides behind "that test was always red."
5. **F-08 and F-06 edit the same function.** If F-08 were assigned as written, that engineer would "fix" `score_answer` — code that already works — while the F-06 owner changes thresholds in the same function. A stale finding plus a real one in one function is a collision waiting to happen.
6. **Test-suite contention.** F-11, F-12, F-06's test updates, and an F-08 regression pin all land in a suite that today is a single 8-line file. If everyone appends to `tests/test_score.py`, they conflict; new per-module test files (`test_rubric.py`, `test_run_batch.py`) keep the partition disjoint.
7. **No integration infrastructure.** The repo has no remote (`git config --get remote.origin.url` returns nothing), one branch (`main`), one commit (`f3cac92`), and exists as a single working copy in this workspace. "Several engineers simultaneously" in one working tree is the degenerate failure mode; without per-engineer clones and an agreed integration remote, the parallelism has nowhere to happen.
8. **Guess-divergence on external values.** F-02's endpoint URL, F-05's v3 identifier, and F-03's rubric name are not derivable from the repo (there are no rubric files at all, and `MODEL_ENDPOINTS` URLs are placeholders). Parallel engineers who guess will guess differently — rework risk rather than conflict risk.

**Question 3 — what I would NOT assign as written.**

- **F-08 — do not assign; it describes a bug that does not exist in the committed code.** The finding says `score_answer` "raises on null/empty answers instead of scoring them zero," but `pipeline/score.py:7-9` already reads `if answer is None or not str(answer).strip(): return {"score": 0.0, "empty": True}` — with a comment saying exactly that. The repo's entire history is one commit containing both this code and FINDINGS.md, so no fix landed after the finding was filed; it was wrong (or written against some other version) from the start. Assigning it invites someone to "fix" correct code. Right move: confirm with the reviewer, close it, and add a cheap regression test to pin the behavior.
- **F-04 + F-13 — do not assign as two tickets.** Same root cause in `pages()`; merge into one before anyone starts (details in questions 1–2).
- **F-06 — not an engineering task yet.** "Thresholds are too lenient; tighten them" names no target values, and `PARTIAL_CREDIT_THRESHOLDS = (0.35, 0.65)` is scoring policy: changing it moves every borderline score in future runs and breaks comparability with past results (`score.py:3`). An engineer should not pick the numbers; the rubric owner decides, then the edit is one line.
- **F-07 — needs scoping first.** `MAX_CONCURRENCY = 4` (`run_batch.py:11`) is dead code, but the loop it supposedly limits is fully synchronous — there is no concurrency to apply it to. The finding as written hides a fork: either delete the constant (five minutes) or build real concurrent execution (a design task with ordering implications). Triage must pick a branch before assignment.
- **Lesser flags — F-03 and F-02 are assignable but blocked on information.** F-03 says to point `refusal.txt` at "the rubric name," but no refusal rubric exists anywhere in the repository (no rubric files at all — `DEFAULT_RUBRIC_VERSION` is just a string in `registry.py`), so the name must come from the reviewer. Likewise F-02's correct `aurora-1` endpoint is not in the repo.

**Question 4 — what each engineer needs locally.**

- **A private clone and an integration point.** The repo currently has no remote configured and one local working copy; before parallel work, stand up a shared origin, and have each engineer clone it and branch from `main` (`f3cac92`), one branch per ticket (e.g. `fix/F-04-pagination`).
- **Python 3 and pytest — nothing else.** Every import across the four pipeline modules and tests is stdlib (`json`, `logging`, `pathlib`, `os`; verified by reading all of them), and no `requirements.txt`/`pyproject.toml`/`setup.py` exists. I ran the suite under Python 3.8.3 / pytest 5.4.3.
- **The correct test invocation.** There are no `__init__.py` files and no installed package, so bare `pytest` fails at collection with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pipeline'` (verified). Run `python -m pytest` from the repo root (which puts the root on `sys.path`), or equivalently `PYTHONPATH=. pytest`.
- **Knowledge of the baseline and triage outcomes.** Everyone must know before starting that `test_full_credit` is red on a clean checkout, that F-04/F-13 are one ticket, that F-08 is closed, and what the F-06/F-07/F-03/F-02 decisions were.
- **Environment details.** `tests/conftest.py:4` reads a `RESULTS_DB` env var (default `/var/tmp/llm-scoring/results.db`); nothing uses it today (verified by grep), but setting it to a workspace-local path is cheap insurance. Also, the repo has no `.gitignore`, so running tests will leave `__pycache__`/`.pytest_cache` as untracked noise — I observed pytest 5.4.3 write `tests/__pycache__` even with bytecode suppression — so engineers should know not to commit those (or a `.gitignore` should be added in phase 0).
- **No network, credentials, or external data.** The pipeline is offline, fixtures (`eval_set.jsonl`, `scratch_set.jsonl`) are in-repo and tiny, and the `MODEL_ENDPOINTS` URLs are `example.com` placeholders nothing calls.

## Actions

In order:

1. `ls -la` of the workspace + `Glob **/*` — workspace contains 14 unrelated repos; identified candidates.
2. `Glob **/FINDINGS.md` and read workspace `README.md` — only `outputs-review/` has a FINDINGS.md; the README describes it as "offline scoring pipeline with a findings backlog," matching the task.
3. Read `outputs-review/FINDINGS.md` — all 14 findings (F-01–F-14). Ran `find` over `outputs-review` — the repo has 13 files: 4 pipeline modules, 2 prompts, 2 fixtures, 2 test files, README, FINDINGS.md.
4. Read `outputs-review/README.md` (confirms repo purpose), `pipeline/run_batch.py` (confirmed F-04/F-13 are the same floor-division bug in `pages()`, F-07 dead constant, F-14 payload logging), `pipeline/registry.py` (confirmed F-02, F-05, F-09).
5. Read `pipeline/score.py` (found F-08 already handled in code; confirmed F-06 thresholds exist) and `pipeline/rubric.py` (confirmed F-01).
6. Read `prompts/grading_system.txt` (confirmed F-10), `prompts/refusal.txt` (confirmed F-03 wording; noted no refusal rubric exists anywhere in the repo), `fixtures/eval_set.jsonl` (confirmed `aurora-1` reference for F-02), `tests/test_score.py` and `tests/conftest.py` (confirmed F-11/F-12 test gaps; found `RESULTS_DB` env var).
7. `git status && git branch -a && git log --oneline --all` in `outputs-review` — single branch `main`, clean tree, single commit `f3cac92`.
8. `git show --stat HEAD` and `git config --get remote.origin.url` — the one commit contains both the code and FINDINGS.md (so F-08's mismatch is not explained by a later fix); no remote is configured. `ls`/`find` for `__init__.py`, `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py` — none exist.
9. Read `fixtures/scratch_set.jsonl`. Ran `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 -B -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q` — **the suite is red on a clean checkout**: `tests/test_score.py::test_full_credit` fails with `assert 0.0 == 1.0`. `git status --porcelain` afterwards confirmed this run wrote nothing.
10. `Grep` for `registry|DEFAULT_|MODEL_ENDPOINTS|MAX_CONCURRENCY|RESULTS_DB` across `*.py` — nothing imports `registry.py` (its three findings are config-only), and `RESULTS_DB` is referenced only in `conftest.py`. 11. I removed that directory — an artifact of my own command, not repository content — and verified with `git status --porcelain` that the tree is back to its exact original state. No repository file was created, modified, or deleted.

No guides, playbooks, or reference documents shaped my approach; everything above came from the repository itself.

sections.answers:
**Question 1 — division of work and ordering.**

The backlog maps onto files like this (verified by reading each file):

| Files | Findings |
|---|---|
| `pipeline/run_batch.py` | F-04, F-07, F-13, F-14 (+ F-12's test targets it) |
| `pipeline/rubric.py` | F-01 (+ F-11's test targets it) |
| `pipeline/registry.py` | F-02, F-05, F-09 |
| `pipeline/score.py` | F-06, F-08 |
| `prompts/refusal.txt`, `prompts/grading_system.txt` | F-03, F-10 |
| `tests/` | F-11, F-12 |

I would run a short triage phase first, then fan out four parallel streams, then a small second wave.

**Phase 0 — triage before anyone is assigned anything (lead + reviewer, under an hour).** Merge F-04 and F-13 into one ticket (they are the same bug: `pages()` at `pipeline/run_batch.py:14-18` computes `n_pages = total // PAGE_SIZE` and yields only full pages, so the trailing partial page is silently dropped — F-04 describes the mechanism, F-13 the observed symptom). Close F-08 as stale (see question 3). Send four questions out: target values for F-06, scope for F-07, the canonical refusal-rubric name for F-03, and the real `aurora-1` endpoint for F-02. Finally, deal with the fact I verified in step 9: `tests/test_score.py::test_full_credit` fails on an untouched checkout (`assert 0.0 == 1.0`, because `Rubric.match_ratio` does a naive substring check and the criterion string "mentions the export button" never appears in the answer). That failure is in no finding, but it must be fixed — or at least filed and explicitly acknowledged — before parallel work starts, because a red baseline destroys everyone's ability to tell their regressions from pre-existing breakage.

**Wave 1 — four parallel streams, partitioned strictly by file so no two engineers ever edit the same file:**

- **Engineer A — `pipeline/run_batch.py` (the hot spot):** F-04/F-13 (fix `pages()` to yield the final partial page), then F-12 (the pagination boundary test — exact multiple of `PAGE_SIZE`, plus one extra row — placed in a new `tests/test_run_batch.py`), then F-14 (change `run_batch.py:27` to log only `row.get("id")`, not the full payload). Four of the fourteen findings live in this 29-line file; giving them all to one owner converts guaranteed merge conflicts into a simple sequence. F-12 and F-04/13 belong to the same person for a second reason: the test is the acceptance criterion for the fix (write it failing, fix, watch it pass).
- **Engineer B — `pipeline/rubric.py`:** F-01 (join multi-line criteria in `Rubric.parse`, `rubric.py:9-11`, which currently keeps only lines starting with `-` and drops continuation lines), then F-11 (edge-case parse tests — empty lines, nested dashes — in a new `tests/test_rubric.py`). Same fix-plus-its-test pairing.
- **Engineer C — `pipeline/registry.py`:** F-09 immediately (`DEFAULT_DATASET` at `registry.py:11` points at `fixtures/eval_set_2025.jsonl`, which does not exist; `fixtures/eval_set.jsonl` does), then F-02 and F-05 as soon as triage supplies the endpoint URL and confirms the v3 rubric identifier. These are three one-line edits in an 11-line file that nothing else imports (verified by grep), so they are trivially safe — but only if one person owns the file.
- **Engineer D — prompts:** F-10 immediately (add the cite-your-criterion instruction to `prompts/grading_system.txt`), F-03 when the rubric name arrives (`prompts/refusal.txt`). Text-only, zero code coupling. D can also add the F-08 regression test pinning the null/empty-scores-zero behavior of `score.py:6-9`.

**Wave 2 — decision-gated items, after answers land:** F-06 (replace `PARTIAL_CREDIT_THRESHOLDS` at `score.py:3` with the agreed values, plus test updates) goes to whoever frees up first — nobody else touches `score.py` in wave 1 once F-08 is closed. F-07 goes to Engineer A only, after F-04/13 has merged, because whatever "apply MAX_CONCURRENCY" turns into will restructure the same loop the pagination fix just changed.

The ordering logic in one line: triage first because the backlog as written contains a duplicate, a stale item, and two undecided items — fanning out before fixing that guarantees wasted work; within streams, fixes and their covering tests are sequenced under one owner; across streams order doesn't matter, which is exactly what the file-based partition buys.

**Question 2 — risks of parallelizing, and what in this backlog creates them.**

1. **Single-file contention in `pipeline/run_batch.py`.** Four findings (F-04, F-07, F-13, F-14) plus F-12's test all target one 29-line file. A naive one-finding-per-engineer split puts three or four people in it simultaneously — textual merge conflicts at minimum.
2. **Duplicate assignment of the same bug.** F-04 and F-13 are one defect described twice (I verified both point at the `pages()` remainder drop). Handed to two engineers, you get two competing rewrites of the same function, and the second merge either conflicts or silently double-applies.
3. **Semantic (not just textual) conflict between F-07 and F-04/F-13.** "Applying" `MAX_CONCURRENCY` means restructuring the sequential loop in `run()` (`run_batch.py:21-29`). Done concurrently with the pagination fix by a different person, a concurrency refactor can reintroduce the dropped-tail bug or change result ordering (`results` currently preserves input order) even if git merges cleanly.
4. **The red baseline poisons everyone's signal.** `tests/test_score.py::test_full_credit` fails on a clean checkout (verified: `assert 0.0 == 1.0`). Every engineer running tests before their first change sees a failure they didn't cause; the F-06 owner, editing `score.py`, is especially likely to burn time thinking they broke it — or worse, a real regression hides behind "that test was always red."
5. **F-08 and F-06 edit the same function.** If F-08 were assigned as written, that engineer would "fix" `score_answer` — code that already works — while the F-06 owner changes thresholds in the same function. A stale finding plus a real one in one function is a collision waiting to happen.
6. **Test-suite contention.** F-11, F-12, F-06's test updates, and an F-08 regression pin all land in a suite that today is a single 8-line file. If everyone appends to `tests/test_score.py`, they conflict; new per-module test files (`test_rubric.py`, `test_run_batch.py`) keep the partition disjoint.
7. **No integration infrastructure.** The repo has no remote (`git config --get remote.origin.url` returns nothing), one branch (`main`), one commit (`f3cac92`), and exists as a single working copy in this workspace. "Several engineers simultaneously" in one working tree is the degenerate failure mode; without per-engineer clones and an agreed integration remote, the parallelism has nowhere to happen.
8. **Guess-divergence on external values.** F-02's endpoint URL, F-05's v3 identifier, and F-03's rubric name are not derivable from the repo (there are no rubric files at all, and `MODEL_ENDPOINTS` URLs are placeholders). Parallel engineers who guess will guess differently — rework risk rather than conflict risk.

**Question 3 — what I would NOT assign as written.**

- **F-08 — do not assign; it describes a bug that does not exist in the committed code.** The finding says `score_answer` "raises on null/empty answers instead of scoring them zero," but `pipeline/score.py:7-9` already reads `if answer is None or not str(answer).strip(): return {"score": 0.0, "empty": True}` — with a comment saying exactly that. The repo's entire history is one commit containing both this code and FINDINGS.md, so no fix landed after the finding was filed; it was wrong (or written against some other version) from the start. Assigning it invites someone to "fix" correct code. Right move: confirm with the reviewer, close it, and add a cheap regression test to pin the behavior.
- **F-04 + F-13 — do not assign as two tickets.** Same root cause in `pages()`; merge into one before anyone starts (details in questions 1–2).
- **F-06 — not an engineering task yet.** "Thresholds are too lenient; tighten them" names no target values, and `PARTIAL_CREDIT_THRESHOLDS = (0.35, 0.65)` is scoring policy: changing it moves every borderline score in future runs and breaks comparability with past results (`score.py:3`). An engineer should not pick the numbers; the rubric owner decides, then the edit is one line.
- **F-07 — needs scoping first.** `MAX_CONCURRENCY = 4` (`run_batch.py:11`) is dead code, but the loop it supposedly limits is fully synchronous — there is no concurrency to apply it to. The finding as written hides a fork: either delete the constant (five minutes) or build real concurrent execution (a design task with ordering implications). Triage must pick a branch before assignment.
- **Lesser flags — F-03 and F-02 are assignable but blocked on information.** F-03 says to point `refusal.txt` at "the rubric name," but no refusal rubric exists anywhere in the repository (no rubric files at all — `DEFAULT_RUBRIC_VERSION` is just a string in `registry.py`), so the name must come from the reviewer. Likewise F-02's correct `aurora-1` endpoint is not in the repo.

**Question 4 — what each engineer needs locally.**

- **A private clone and an integration point.** The repo currently has no remote configured and one local working copy; before parallel work, stand up a shared origin, and have each engineer clone it and branch from `main` (`f3cac92`), one branch per ticket (e.g. `fix/F-04-pagination`).
- **Python 3 and pytest — nothing else.** Every import across the four pipeline modules and tests is stdlib (`json`, `logging`, `pathlib`, `os`; verified by reading all of them), and no `requirements.txt`/`pyproject.toml`/`setup.py` exists. I ran the suite under Python 3.8.3 / pytest 5.4.3.
- **The correct test invocation.** There are no `__init__.py` files and no installed package, so bare `pytest` fails at collection with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pipeline'` (verified). Run `python -m pytest` from the repo root (which puts the root on `sys.path`), or equivalently `PYTHONPATH=. pytest`.
- **Knowledge of the baseline and triage outcomes.** Everyone must know before starting that `test_full_credit` is red on a clean checkout, that F-04/F-13 are one ticket, that F-08 is closed, and what the F-06/F-07/F-03/F-02 decisions were.
- **Environment details.** `tests/conftest.py:4` reads a `RESULTS_DB` env var (default `/var/tmp/llm-scoring/results.db`); nothing uses it today (verified by grep), but setting it to a workspace-local path is cheap insurance. Also, the repo has no `.gitignore`, so running tests will leave `__pycache__`/`.pytest_cache` as untracked noise — I observed pytest 5.4.3 write `tests/__pycache__` even with bytecode suppression — so engineers should know not to commit those (or a `.gitignore` should be added in phase 0).
- **No network, credentials, or external data.** The pipeline is offline, fixtures (`eval_set.jsonl`, `scratch_set.jsonl`) are in-repo and tiny, and the `MODEL_ENDPOINTS` URLs are `example.com` placeholders nothing calls.
sections.confidence and gaps:
- **High confidence** in the finding-to-file map, the F-04/F-13 duplication, F-08 being stale, the dead `MAX_CONCURRENCY`, the missing `eval_set_2025.jsonl`, the missing `aurora-1` mapping, and the test gaps — each is grounded in a file I read or a command whose output is quoted above. The red baseline and the `ModuleNotFoundError` under bare `pytest` were both observed by actually running the suite.
- **Moderate confidence, environment-dependent:** the bare-`pytest` import failure was observed on pytest 5.4.3; newer pytest versions with different rootdir/`sys.path` handling could behave differently. The red test itself is logic-level (a substring check that cannot match), so I'm confident it fails regardless of version.
- **Could not verify:** what "rubric-v3" concretely refers to (no rubric files exist in the repo), the correct `aurora-1` endpoint, the canonical refusal-rubric name, and whether (0.35, 0.65) is genuinely "too lenient" — all four require information from outside the repository, which is exactly why I flagged those findings as blocked-on-info or decision-gated rather than assignable as written. I also can't tell whether F-08 was ever true against some pre-squash version of the code; the single-commit history makes that unknowable, but it doesn't change the conclusion that the current code does not raise.
- **One judgment call left open deliberately:** whether the failing `test_full_credit` indicates a wrong test or a wrong `match_ratio` implementation. I flagged it for triage rather than assuming a side.
sections.next steps: If I were allowed to make changes, in order: (1) run the phase-0 triage — edit FINDINGS.md to merge F-04/F-13, mark F-08 closed-as-stale with a pointer to `score.py:7-9`, and file the red `test_full_credit` as a new finding; (2) send the four questions (F-06 values, F-07 scope, F-03 rubric name, F-02 endpoint) to the reviewer/rubric owner; (3) add a `.gitignore` and set up the shared remote; (4) fix or `xfail` the baseline test so wave 1 starts green; (5) cut the four wave-1 branches and start Engineer A on the pagination fix, since F-04/F-13 is the most serious correctness bug (batch runs silently lose up to `PAGE_SIZE - 1` rows) and F-12 depends on it.
sections.plan: The task: plan how several engineers could clear the 14-finding backlog in `outputs-review/FINDINGS.md` in parallel without collisions, and answer four specific questions. My approach was to (1) locate the right repository in the multi-repo workspace, (2) read the backlog, (3) read every source, prompt, fixture, and test file the findings reference and verify each finding against the actual code rather than trusting the descriptions, (4) inspect git state (branches, history, remote) since that constrains how parallel work is integrated, and (5) establish the test-suite baseline, since "tests pass" is the coordination signal parallel engineers rely on. Verifying every finding first was deliberate: a plan that assigns findings as written is only sound if the findings are accurate, and I found three ways they are not (a duplicate pair, a stale finding, and two decision-shaped findings).
